More shells started falling. One landed as the boys and girls from Vedrana's children's home arrived with their flowers. As quickly as they could, they dropped them on the graves of Vedrana and the baby boy the sniper also murdered. It was time to go. As the family was leaving, the gunners found their range. "Ruza Glavas, the grandmother, was hit in the arm. Reporters tried to stop the bleeding." "Hurry up, another dressing, tourniquet, tight, tight. Get the woman's daughter." "Reporter: Another shell exploded as she was carried to the car. The doctors said they could save Ruza's arm, but that she might lose the use of it. She tried to tell her daughter that she was all right. Svetlana is educationally sub-normal and very dependent on her. At least six mortar rounds landed in or around the graveyard. There were two direct hits just at the time that the children's funerals were due to start. The shooting isn't always this accurate, but the place is attacked nearly every day. There's no question that the Serb gunners are targeting the graveyard to kill civilians. It's hard to find people here who believe the denials made by local Serb leaders. Shells have been landing near civilians all day. Bosnian Government forces are fighting on all fronts around Sarajevo. They claim to have taken ground to the north. It all went on well into the evening. The human cost, as always here, is considerable. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, first of all, is the shelling of the -- the image of the shelling of the funeral that we've just seen, the incident you described at paragraph 37 of your written evidence?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment you'd like to offer on this last clip?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, there's some context I'd like to give. You know, I'm -- by then, I was an experienced reporter, and now, after nearly 20 years later, I'm a very experienced reporter of conflict and I've seen a lot of bad things. But when I see that, I'm still outraged by it, and I'm -- it was a very cruel day for those poor people, it was a very, very cruel and heartless day. Why did I -- why did I think that this shelling was coming from Serb positions? Because -- various things. I was told, for example, by -- previously, before that, because it had happened before, and I subsequently checked again by various people in the UN, that they reckoned -- even some of the military people reckoned even that they knew where it was coming from, in terms of where the shells were landing. It was a -- the Lion's Cemetery was a conspicuous place, and so, you know, I guess everybody knew where it was. After subsequently some people made the accusation that it was staged, that the Bosnian Muslims side were shelling their own positions, shelling their own place, because they knew there would be TV cameras there to cover this quite high-profile funeral, well, I don't buy that, because, apart from anything else, the shelling started long before we arrived. In fact, when I got there, one of the things that went through my mind was -- when told by the grave diggers that shelling had happened, we got all our information there from the grave diggers who were there every day, and I thought -- in fact, I was regretful that we'd missed some of the shelling because it would be hard to illustrate in a piece without it, and then it started again and got closer, and finally that one landed yards away from the grave, yards away from the mother and the grandmother, and it was very fortunate that nobody was killed on that particular occasion. I thought it inflicted terrible cruelty on the people. They were absolutely terrorised, the children as well, by what was going on there. And as I say, it was something that had happened, the grave diggers said, many times before. And you could see as well in the graveyard, the war graves, where they had very simple wooden markers, but the older graves, because it was a previously-used graveyard, had proper headstones and markers, and you could see lumps knocked out of them by shrapnel. And that wasn't just from that day, that was from lots of days. And there was this lion sculpture there and that was damaged as well by shrapnel from shelling. So, you know, it wasn't safe even when you were dead there, in a sense. You were in the ground, and the whole thing could -- you could still be shelled. So it was a regular target, and I had that from numerous different sources, and it was a regular target as well when journalists were nowhere near. So, as I say, I do not buy any kind of argument that that was a show put on for our benefit. I think that it was part of the daily business. And I wouldn't even know if people on the other side knew that that particular funeral was taking place at that particular time, because we actually had to work very hard to find out the times of the funerals, send people up to the graveyard, talk to, you know, the grave diggers, when are they going to bury these people, because we wanted to be there when the funeral happened. So, as I say, my feelings about it are still that even though I am, I suppose you could say, hardened by many years of covering conflict, I am still outraged by those images, and I was at the time, and I continue to be. And I think -- and I would stand by 100 per cent by what I said in that piece, because I think it was based on good and sound information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, would I be able to have these two clips, 40349J, which was the first one, and 40349R as Prosecution exhibits? And, Your Honour, I should note that a small part of 40349R has been previously admitted as P01933.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, is it our practice to expand the previous exhibit? I will consult the Deputy Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it separately with proper notation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They will be exhibit numbers P2077 and 2078 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now to move on to another part or another section of your written evidence, Mr. Bowen. There, you see that you travelled to the eastern enclaves in August of 1992, and in that regard you reached Gorazde. That's at paragraphs 63 -- pardon me, 53 to 61. You've attempted to visit Cerska in February 1993. That's at paragraphs 62 to 67. And you reported on events in Srebrenica and -- you reported on events in Srebrenica in 1995. And I'd like to deal first with your visit to Gorazde in the summer of 1992. Could you tell me, first of all, what prompted the visit?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I had good working relations with UNHCR. Their main co-ordinator there, Larry Hollingworth, told me that he was going to try to get into Gorazde. He asked us if we wanted to come along, and one of the reasons for that was we at that time were the only news organisation there with an armoured Land Rover, because it was going to be a dangerous trip. I wanted to go there because this was a significant town which had been cut off since the beginning of the war. At that point, nobody from the outside world had reached Gorazde since the beginning of the war, so you're talking a period right through to the spring into the late summer, a period of some months. I was interested in the condition of the population, I was interested to see whether the Serb side, having given various assurances, we were told, to the UNHCR, would actually let them through. I was interested to see what we could find there. It was unknown ground, and that was clearly going to be newsworthy --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In Gorazde, did you make observations of the humanitarian situation in the town?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was a quick trip. We were in and out in the course of one day. We got in there in the, I guess, early-ish morning. I think it was probably -- it was fully light, it was summer, maybe it was 9.00, 10.00 in the morning, 11.00 perhaps, by the time we got in there, and we were out of there by late afternoon. So it was a quick trip, maybe even a bit less than that time, maybe more like three or four hours. Anyway, yes, I did see the state of the population. To start with, as we went in, as we entered Gorazde, people -- the streets were absolutely empty, to start with. The UNHCR had negotiated a local cease-fire, but there had been shelling until -- because we could hear it, until not long before that. We -- let me try and get this right in my own mind. Yes, what happened was that we went into the -- that street. People started emerging from their houses. And it was the middle of the summer, but they were all white. They hadn't been sunburnt, suntanned. They'd clearly been sheltering most of the time for all of that period, and they looked absolutely desperate. The atmosphere there, once they realised that the UN and French and Ukrainian UN troops had arrived, became very cheerful, though there was still emotion, people crying with relief and so on. I think they thought that the UN people were there to stay. They brought out drinks. It was the kind of atmosphere that I could imagine from having seen video of towns in Normandy being liberated in 1944, with soldiers throwing down packets of cigarettes, locals coming out with drinks and passing them up to the soldiers. It was -- you know, it was a -- for a while, it was quite a -- once it sunk in, what was happening, quite a carnival atmosphere. We went off to see what we could do while they were unloading the supplies, and there was a building that was being used -- there was a little hospital quite near the center of town, and while -- we went over there, myself and the cameraman, and while we were there we saw some of the, really, most horrible things I've seen up to then and since. The worst of it was a young child - I said it was a girl, but I think it was a boy, I got that slightly wrong - having shrapnel taken out of the child's body without anaesthetic. It was an absolutely horrendous sight. The child was screaming in pain. The doctor, afterwards, when I interviewed him, he was wearing a white coat but he was pale, and you could see, above his heart -- you absolutely -- you could see his white coat, you know, moving, like that, up and down. You could see his heart was beating so fast, it wasn't that he was thin, it was making an impression on his coat, on his white overall, because, you know, he said he felt like a butcher taking out shrapnel, without anesthetic, out of a child who was less two years old, maybe more like 18 months old, a small child. It was a really grim sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. I'd like to play your report on the situation in Gorazde and then ask you a couple of questions on that, and that is 65 ter 45372B.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Reporter: It was the UN's third attempt to get to Gorazde. Last time, they were ambushed, so they were ready for trouble." "If, in fact, we come under mortar or shelling, we go forward. We go forward like the clappers of hell. If we come under fighting, we get out and we try to hide. It's as simple as that." "Reporter: But we reached Gorazde safely, moving cautiously through the burnt and empty suburbs on the edge of the town. Only 500 yards or so after the last Serb position, the lead armoured personnel carrier pushed its way through, suspending if not ending a siege that had lasted 146 days. The UN had tried to warn the people that the convoy was coming. It had been worried that the defenders of Gorazde might open fire. But we were welcomed with great emotion and relief. Most of them couldn't do much more than cry." "You can see, you can see. I cannot speak." "Reporter: Since the war started, the people here have been cut off from the outside world, but they wanted us to show that despite everything, they're still human beings who are trying to hang on to their self-respect. It's been hard, though. They said there was shelling every day. Until they saw the UN soldiers, most of them had been too frightened even to go outside. In the few minutes since we've been in Gorazde, the people have started coming out of their cellars and out of their shelters. The arrival of the UN convoy is the first good news they've had since the siege began. The Serbs around Gorazde had agreed to stop the shelling to let the convoy through, but wounded men were still coming in from ground fighting on the fringes of the town. "At the hospital were more of the war's latest victims. Most of them were civilians who'd been hurt just before the cease-fire started. This 15-year-old boy was hit by a mortar fragment. They were trying to do the best they could for Ana Djebo, a three-year-old girl with grievous wounds, but the doctors had no proper anaesthetic. They used alcohol to clean the wound and a small amount of morphine to kill some of the pain. It's not enough. A nurse had to hold Ana down while the doctor went on with the operation. They used the light from the camera because their own wasn't strong enough. "If Ana survives, she'll be told her parents are dead. They were killed by the mortar which wounded her. Ana's doctor was distraught. He said he was sweating not because it was hot but because he was appalled by what he had to do every day. In the next bed, a man was having shrapnel taken out of his shoulder, again without anaesthetic. All their families can do is watch. The doctors say they performed hundreds of operations like this. There's a small amount of local anaesthetic which is reserved for amputations. The patients are conscious throughout. They cannot give the amputees the blood transfusions and special care they need. Without it, most of them die. In the town, they were unloading food and medical supplies. None of it will last very long. They worked as fast as they could in case they were attacked, but the cease-fire held. It looked as though the mission had been a success. It started to go wrong on the journey back to Sarajevo. On a remote road in the forest, a spot perfect for ambush, mines were discovered and the convoy stopped." "Well, it's a very dangerous stretch of the road. If I wanted to park the convoy, this would be one of the last places I would park it." "Reporter: French combat engineers cleared the road. They reached the convoy after it had been stranded for a night and a day. The UN will need to take mine experts and perhaps more armour if they try to get to Gorazde again. No one knows who planted the mines, but they were intended to kill UN personnel. They were blown up safely before anyone was hurt. Fighting we could hear for about an hour and a half had more serious results. Later, the Serbs said the UN troops had been close to a surprise attack by Muslims who'd used the convoy as cover. It was their worst setback, they said, since the siege started. They showed us the bodies of eight dead Serb fighters. They might not let another convoy through. But the people of Gorazde need much more than humanitarian aid. They need peace, and there's no chance of that. The shelling started again soon after we left. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC News, Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bowen, in this report you referred to the fact that this was, to your understanding, the UN's third attempt to enter Gorazde, you referred to a siege that had lasted 146 days, and you referred to Serbs around Gorazde who at that time had agreed to let the convoy through. Now, this situation, as reflected in these comments, did you see that repeated in any of the eastern enclaves later in the war?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, but can I just deal with one thing before I answer that question? It was simply that I said that we entered in the early morning. On reflection, and that's why I hesitated just after I said that, I think it was more late morning than early morning. That was just a small point for accuracy. Yes, I mean, I think that pattern of surrounding and besieging those enclaves was repeated in them right towards the end. The defenders of Gorazde became much better organised as time went by, and the Serbs never succeeded in getting into Gorazde, though there was, I heard at the time, and I've had it confirmed to me since by UN soldiers who were in there, various special forces people, they said that there was heavy fighting that they saw themselves, and I think that's all been well documented now. Gorazde was well organised, and they held out right to the end. Srebrenica was a different matter in 1995, but that generalised pattern of surrounding it, exerting military pressure, and trying to push in and take territory and break through the perimeter of those enclaves which had been declared UN safe areas as well, of course, that was a pattern that was repeated, I think, throughout the enclaves for the duration of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your written evidence refers to your attempt to enter Cerska in February 1993. Did you -- were you aware of a similar situation as regards Cerska?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, we were aware that there was an enclave. We were aware that they had received not a great deal in terms of aid. The UNHCR and Larry Hollingworth, the guy with the white beard who was in that piece, was keen to try to repeat what they'd done in Gorazde in Cerska. And it was the winter, it was extremely cold, but they didn't succeed in getting the convoy, and despite having -- he actually said, We've got all the assurances that we need, we've get the papers, we've got the promises, and we will be able to get in there. But on that occasion, we had an escort of the French Foreign Legion, but we were stuck in Zvornik for at least two nights, three days, two nights, maybe even three nights, I can't remember precisely, and we didn't go in. And then, ironically, what we discovered was at that particular point, Cerska actually fell to Serb forces, and then the Serbs took us to see some of the aftermath of that. They claimed, for example, that bodies they'd unearthed from graves were bodies of dead Serbs. They also said that there was -- they showed us a post with a piece of metal on it and said Serbs were chained to this. But to me, it looked like a fence post, and I thought, well, how would they know that. So I took that with some degree of skepticism. But I did see there was a certain irony in that the UNHCR and the relief people were of the people that they'd been given permission to get into the enclave at a time that it was being militarily invested by the Serbs, leading to its fall.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Speaking of the fall of Cerska, did you become aware of the ultimate fate of the civilian population of that area? Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Not in detail. I think that they -- those that survived left, had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to play you now another one of your reports, 65 ter 40349T, which I believe dates from April of 1993. And I'll have some questions for you at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you tender the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was going to go through it all at once. But, yes, please, Your Honour, 45372B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will be Exhibit P2079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Reporter: Each attempt to evacuate civilians from Srebrenica so far has ended in chaos. Desperate people have rushed the UN lorries. Some of the weakest have been killed in the crush. But the UNHCR, it seems, now believes it's found a better way to do it. It says it has 60 trucks on standby. The plan is to take 20 into the town every day partially loaded with food. On their way out, they'll evacuate between 1.000 and 1500 people. The UNHCR hopes to rescue up to 15.000, a little less than half the population of the town. UNHCR denies it's assisting in the Serb's policy of ethnic cleansing." "The people we are evacuating from Srebrenica have already been ethnically cleansed because they are coming from areas that have already fallen under Serbian control. They are not people from Srebrenica, they arrive... "Reporter: From the villages around..." "From the villages around and also from Konjevic Polje, from Cerska, areas that were fall under Serbian control a couple of weeks ago." "Reporter: The Serbs, who surround Srebrenica and control who goes in and out, seem to be stepping up their offensives in the area. Privately, aid workers believe that the fall of the town is only a matter of time and that the civilian population must be evacuated before that happens. The next 48 hours, the UNHCR believes, will be crucial."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that report, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that refresh any recollection as to what happened to the civilian population of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that, you know, it was apparent from the statement there by the UN official, the guy in the smart shirt and tie and jacket, that many of them moved on to Srebrenica, that they got out and, no doubt, went across the hills and across the fields to get there through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where did that film -- or do you know where that film of the truckloads of civilians came from, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: We received that through an agency. I don't remember the precise origin. I was not, myself, in Srebrenica, so I wasn't involved in the filming of it. Srebrenica was a very difficult place to get into. In fact, I think only one person -- only one journalist succeeded in doing so during the war. But during that period where there was quite a bit of coming and going with the UNHCR, there were pictures that were shot, as you see, from inside it, and, you know, one of the significances of Srebrenica was that it was big. There were 30.000 civilians in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please, 40349T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2080, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bowen, your written evidence indicates that you reported on the fall of the enclave of Srebrenica in 1995, although you reported from Sarajevo. I'd like to play -- and that's at paragraph 68. I'd like to play some of those reports now for you, the first being 65 ter 45372C.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Reporter: The Dutch UN peacekeepers, who are effectively prisoners, could only watch as Bosnian Serb soldiers perform for the cameras, handing out chocolate. General Ratko Mladic, commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb Army, addressed the crowd. Don't be afraid, he said, buses will take you to Muslim territory, women and children first. Nobody will hurt you. The crowd of women and old men chorussed thank you as he went about his business. Today, the business has been ethnic cleansing. Around 30.000 people, almost all of them Muslims, were trapped in the enclave. Tonight, the pictures showed no Bosnian men of fighting age. The UN says all males over 16 are being interviewed as suspected war criminals. Successful action against Muslim terrorists continues, the headlines said. Radovan Karadzic, leader of the Bosnian Serbs, was in the studio. This, he said, is the latest example of the superiority of the Serbian people. Threats from the international community mean nothing to us. If NATO attacks, we must defend. He said that if Muslims in Zepa and Gorazde, the other safe areas in Eastern Bosnia, don't give up their weapons, the Serbs must attack. And as for people leaving Srebrenica, he said that nobody was forcing them to go."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bowen, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was one that I did. And I think that the sound that was lost off the beginning said that that was a report from Pale TV. That's where we got the pictures. We were able -- I was in Sarajevo when Srebrenica fell, and we were technically able to monitor the output of Pale Television and record it off air, which is what we did, which is where we got that material. So that was material shot by them. And as I say, I explained the provenance of the pictures, I think, at the beginning of the piece, but that's what was lost from the soundtrack. So, yes, I do recognise that report, and I remember doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You noted, in this report, that no men of fighting age were shown in these pictures. Did you attribute any significance to that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, I did, I did attribute significance to that, and the significance was that they had been taken somewhere to be imprisoned or dealt with in some particular way. And I -- there was that quote of them being questioned. I was on the lookout for things like that. It occurred to me, as I was watching the pictures, very strongly, that I thought to myself, Hang on a minute, where are the guys, where are the men, where are the young men, especially? Because there had been accounts over the previous years of -- and those kinds of situations where a group of Muslims would fall into the hands of the Serbs, that men of fighting age would be separated out, I think that there was something in my brain that was looking for that, and so it clicked very quickly, when I was watching Pale TV, that -- that there weren't men of fighting age in the pictures. So, naturally, I wondered what had happened to them, and I thought it was worthy of mention, therefore, in my script.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before dealing with this one as an exhibit, we'll go on to the next report I would like to show you, and that's 45372E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, can we know the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was when -- I don't have the dates in front of me, but it would have been July 1995, I think. It was summer of 1995. I can't recall, off-hand, the precise date of the fall of the enclave of Srebrenica, but it would have been done -- that particular one would have been done a few days after the actual fall of it, because it took a day or two for the pictures to get out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I'm pretty sure that would have been July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Reporter: Two and a half thousand refugees are now congregated at Tuzla Airport. They're dehydrated and exhausted. The UN is running out of room for them and so far it can offer only the most basic help, but it's worried that in the next few days it may have to feed and shelter as many as 40.000 others, once the Serbs complete the ethnic cleansing of what was supposed to be the safe area of Srebrenica. They're still streaming over the front-line, almost all of them women and children. Their husbands, brothers, and fathers have been left behind for interrogation as suspected war criminals."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Bowen, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not 100 per cent, but I think those -- quite a lot of our pictures there, because we went up to Tuzla to try and see refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have these two as the next Prosecution exhibits, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P2081 and P2082 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder whether we will also be admitting footages made by others, where Mr. Bowen wasn't at the moment, and all we get is his interpretation of the footages that we are looking at. And I would like to know who the authors of the footages is. Are we admitting the way Mr. Bowen interprets other people's work or do we only admit his own work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Karadzic. You do not challenge this is a report made by Mr. Bowen, but you are asking who took these films. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way I understood it is this: Mr. Bowen told us that he received footages from other agencies, and provided those footages with his own comments and then distributed them for airing. Could the Prosecutor clarify that with the witness? And depending on the answer we receive, we will probably have an objection to the admission of such material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually don't quite understand, Your Honour, because in respect of the first clip, P2081, Mr. Bowen said clearly in his evidence that that was picked up from Pale TV. In respect of the second clip, Mr. Bowen said, We went up to Tuzla, and that was their film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was my understanding. Could you add to that, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I have a recollection of being in that tunnel that was featured in the -- in those pictures that people were walking through. And I think we went up to Tuzla because we felt it was important to get some first-hand testimony from people who were coming out of Srebrenica, because, you know, as you know, geographically, it's not a big distance between Srebrenica and Tuzla, so people were walking out. And so the provenance of those pictures, I felt, was therefore clear. And as I said earlier on, the material from Bosnian Serb TV we recorded off air in our office at the television station in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bowen. We don't see any problem in admitting these, and then the issue you raised may be a matter you can raise during your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We actually -- we actually have some more footages from 1993 that was also taken over from some other agency. I would have really appreciated if I could know what it was that Mr. Bowen actually saw for himself, what his own material is, rather than hearing his comments on the material of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a matter you should explore during your cross-examination. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bowen, following your reports on the fall of Srebrenica, did you do any further reports on the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think I did something about Zepa. We did -- you know, getting information was difficult because we were unable to travel to them. We did put in requests to the Bosnian Serb press office to be able to travel to the east to do first-hand reporting, and we didn't get a positive response. We got information from radio amateurs in Sarajevo. We also had statements from the Sarajevo government. Haris Silajdzic often came to the television station -- well, he often spoke to us, but he came -- at the time of Srebrenica, he came to the TV station to express his grave concern about what was going on. And also we got information from UNPROFOR, who, of course, had their Dutch UN troops there who were feeding out information, and some of that, not all, I'm certain, but some of that was passed on to us by UNPROFOR people in Sarajevo, who expressed their strongest concern about what was happening there, their really strongest concern. And they said some of it on camera openly, but away from the camera they were very depressed about their failure to protect the people of Srebrenica, and very concerned as well about what was happening to the men of fighting age.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just mentioned in your first sentence that you thought you did something about Zepa, and in that regard I'd like to play a report that you did do about Zepa, 65 ter 45372F.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Reporter: The capture of Zepa is General Ratko Mladic's latest military triumph. A week ago, Bosnian Serb TV broadcast these pictures of what was supposed to be surrender talks to back up premature Serb claims that they had taken the enclave. Now the UN says the general has finally done it on the day its own human rights tribunal indicted him and Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader, for genocide and crimes against humanity. Both men are being held responsible for atrocities against civilians and for taking hostage UN personnel. But despite that, the UN is still negotiating with them to rescue civilians from Zepa." "We will get a ruling on that from the UN in New York, I am sure. In the meantime, we will take the view that it is better that this dialogue goes on in the interest of what is happening out there than it to be cut at this stage." "Reporter: Haris Silajdzic, the Bosnian prime minister, wants Western governments to do more than deplore war crimes, he wants them to take sides." "Genocide is going on right now in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The problem is that the Western governments would not recognise that fact, would not evoke the genocide Geneva Convention, because it entails some responsibility and some obligation." "Reporter: To avoid a repeat of the scenes that followed the fall of Srebrenica, he wants UN protection for refugees from Zepa. The UN now has documented evidence of attacks on refugees from Srebrenica by Serb soldiers which will be passed on to the International War Crimes Tribunal. This morning, the UN spokesman read extracts from the file." "A number of those interviewed reported seeing between six and ten bodies of people who had been executed by having their throats cut. Persons evacuated on the convoy also have given statements relating to young women being forcibly taken from the displaced persons by Serb soldiers." "Reporter: In Zenica, in Central Bosnia, the UN is preparing the supplies to avoid what it has called a humanitarian catastrophe. They hope they'll be ready for what looks like a certainty of a huge influx of refugees from Zepa. And with French troops now alongside the British on Mount Igman above Sarajevo, the UN's own security has much improved. The Bosnians are waiting to see if the foreign soldiers can do the same for them. Now that Zepa has gone, the enclave of Bihac is the UN safe area most at risk. It's probably where the UN's resolve will next be tested. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that report, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to these and the other reports that we've seen over the course of your testimony today, could you give us an idea over what area or areas the BBC was broadcast? Where were your reports disseminated?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, it was before the days of widespread satellite broadcasting that we use now commonplace, but things were available by satellite. We would -- our main audience at that time was domestic BBC News. I think by 1995, BBC World was just beginning, so they would have broadcast it, I think. I'll have to check that, but they were starting around 1995. I think they'd already got going. And things would also get picked up by local stations. It was possible, in a TV station technically at that time, and not difficult, to pull reports and news programmes off satellites and then re-broadcast them yourself, and not on a regular basis, but, you know, from time to time -- well, not on a programme basis, but fairly regularly, from time to time, I should say is more accurate, our reports and those of other broadcasters would get recorded locally by one or other of the different TV stations and then disseminated; I mean, in a different location in 1991, during the Croatian war, I remember visiting Borovo Selo, where there were Serbs fighting or surrounded by Croats, and they were very suspicious of us, to start with, because they had seen a piece that I had done which had been re-broadcast on Serbian TV, and they couldn't speak English so they didn't understand what I was saying in it, but they didn't like the images. So it took a few days to try to, successfully in the end, win their confidence. Funny enough, they -- I won their confidence when they saw another piece that I had broadcast which they liked a bit more. And that pattern, I think, continued through the Bosnian war as well, that reports by the BBC, by CNN, by other international broadcasters were picked up and re-broadcast locally, as I say, from time to time, not every night.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, 65 ter 45372F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Bowen, do you remember or recognise where it was that Mr. Karadzic was drinking a shot of something like alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't there when that was shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was from the Serbian TV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would have picked that up, because we at the same time -- and I should have added that as well as that night when we recorded their news programme to get their news from Srebrenica, we recorded their news every night in the hope that we would get some interesting material off it, and that I'm 99.9 per cent certain would have been from that source, because Dr. Karadzic was often featured on Bosnian Serb TV. They would have TV crews that followed him around when he went on public events like that particular thing. And so we -- that's where we would have got that material from, because we certainly weren't privy to following -- at that particular time, following his movements through the area that the Bosnian Serbs controlled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted as Exhibit P2083.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just briefly on to the final area, Mr. Bowen. In your written evidence, at paragraph 70 and 71, you referred to meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, and in particular a meeting with Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic in Geneva. And in that regard, I'd like to play you 65 ter 40349U, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Reporter: Tonight, the Muslim leader, Alija Izetbegovic, was showing the strain after his first meetings with the Bosnian Serbs since the war began. There'll be more tomorrow, and there's no deal in sight." "Are you optimistic?" "Alija Izetbegovic: Talks are going on tomorrow. Maybe. I have to be optimistic." "Reporter: A mile away, the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, Radovan Karadzic, is spending an evening with his closest advisers." "Radovan Karadzic: This is the beginning, this is not final map and we have to correct..." "Reporter: They are assessing the new map of Bosnia, decentralising power. Its adoption is considered vital if the talks are to succeed. No side here has accepted it yet. Mr. Karadzic said the Muslims never would." "Radovan Karadzic: ... and they are hoping for military intervention. They hope international community will come and help them establish an Islamic state in the middle of Europe. That's what Mr. Izetbegovic thinks." "Reporter: General Ratko Mladic, the Serbs' military commander, showed us pictures of what he said were Muslim and Croatian war crimes against Serb civilians. There's no goodwill here and no trust."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, is this video we've just seen a video of the interview with Dr. Karadzic you have set out in your statement at paragraphs 70 and 71?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I arranged to see Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic in a suite that they were using in the Intercontinental Hotel in Geneva. Also, that list scene with President Izetbegovic, that was filmed in the Hotel President in Geneva, where his delegation was staying. And on both cases it was something that we filmed ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you make -- on seeing these photographs that were displayed in this video report, did you raise any queries or make any comment to Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. He had pictures of corpses that had been exhumed from various graves, often in a pretty bad state, but it was clear that a lot of them -- well, most of them were wearing green uniforms and big boots. So I said to him, They look like soldiers to me. And he said, No, they're Serb farmers, Serb farmers wear green clothing and big boots. He maintained that they were civilians. They also gave me a similar video -- a similar thing, which was a video, to take with me, a VHS tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you attribute any credence to his response to you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, they were clearly dead people. I thought, considering that the men were of military age and they were dressed in what appeared to be military uniforms, I found it hard to believe that they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could that be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2084, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, that concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Karadzic, it's now time for you to cross-examine the witness. But given the time, however, if you so wish, we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It's okay with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay to have a break? We'll do that. We'll break for half an hour and resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bowen. If you agree, I would like to start with the last video-clip. I'm grateful to His Excellency Mr. Kwon for his question related to the footage that had to do with me. For what purposes did you include that in your footage on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Are you referring, sir, to the picture of you having a toast with the guys in the field?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: We used it because we needed a picture of you. You were there, in a rural environment, and I think it followed on visually quite nicely from General Mladic also having a toast with the people with whom he was negotiating. It seemed to reflect the mood. And also, I think, it was a contemporaneous picture, as far as I recall, that we took off Pale TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think that's fair to your viewers, not to mention this Court, to associate two events that are a month apart, and two locations, at that? You realised, from TV Pale, that this is the beginning of the harvesting season, and that is what I am congratulating them on, on the fact that the harvest has started. That was the beginning of June, whereas you are dealing with Zepa in July. I realise you want to achieve a certain effect, but we are dealing with a criminal case here. Do you think it is fair to edit it this way?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was fair. I don't know that there was a month between the two pictures. I'll have to take your word on that. I think it was fair. Personally, I mean, if you're referring to the fact that there might be a suggestion that there was something pejorative about seeing you having a small toast with the farmers, I mean, I have no problem with that at all. I don't see the difficulty in that, and I don't suppose our viewers would have. I think it -- it was a more interesting picture, seeing you with the farmers, than seeing you sitting behind a desk in the office. I don't think it was unfair to show you going about your business in your position that you had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can understand your concern for your viewers, Mr. Bowen, and that you want them to enjoy what they're seeing. However, what you are implying here is that my toast has something to do with the taking of Zepa. You've actually linked the two. Is that fair and is that permissible?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I wasn't going out of my way to link the two in any sense of putting a political message in there. There was a visual link between someone raising a glass in one location and someone raising a glass in another location. I don't think that -- I mean, I hadn't even thought, until you mentioned it, that somehow you could be congratulating General Mladic for what he was doing with -- in that negotiation with those guys, because the pictures clearly showed you with the farmers and they were beginning the harvest. So I don't come away with that impression from the pictures at all, and I can certainly tell you that it was not my intention to give that impression. I hope that in all my dealings with you during those years, that I was as fair as I could be. I, personally, had no interest in trying to be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since my time is limited for this cross-examination, I'm going to do my best to put questions that are as specific as possible and that will allow you to give a yes or no answer, of course, when you allow yourself to do that, so I don't have to ask for more time for this cross-examination. I would like to start with this addendum, this correction to your statement that has to do with firing at those children on the bus. You say: [In English] "I can only presume that at the time I was misinformed about the location of the attack." [Interpretation] You were not on that bus, were you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: At the time of the attack, no, I was not on the bus. And I don't think that I was -- at no point in my reporting did I suggest that I was. I couldn't have been on the bus as well, because the attack happened after the bus had left Bosnian Government-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that you could have been misinformed. If you agree, in wartime there are many ruses, if you agree, and all of that is done in order to vilify the other side; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think ruses are used in wartime, yes, I do. But I think in this particular case, the -- to my mind, there is no dispute about what happened; that the bus was shot at after it had left territory controlled by the Bosnian Government, and the two children on board were killed. The clarification that I mentioned at the beginning of the morning here was that I got the location of where the shooting took place wrong, because it's clear, if we -- we didn't play -- the report was not played, but if you'd seen it, you'd have seen me standing near the "Oslobodjenje" building in Sarajevo, which once I had been there for about another few days, I realised -- I would have realised couldn't possibly have been the location of the shooting because it was controlled by the Bosnian Government. And we had clear pictures, plus testimony of people, that the bus had left that, had gone further down the road, and had crossed through the Bosnian Government check-point, and, in fact, we had in the piece a picture of the bus going through that check-point. So I don't think there's any ruse there, in terms -- what I was misinformed about was the location of the shooters, and that's why I felt it was necessary today to bring that to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I actually wanted to ask you about your sources of information. Who were they, especially with regard to things that you had not seen for yourself? Who informed you, in addition to Silajdzic, who you refer to several times as your source of information, and civilians, and so on and so forth? Where did you get your information from; that you later broadcast, that is?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, as you'll know, sir, journalists don't reveal their sources, but I'm very happy to talk, in general terms, about -- not about individuals, but about the kinds of places that they worked. With Mr. Silajdzic, I was -- I was referring specifically on that occasion to the Srebrenica events, though we did -- I did talk to him on a pretty regular basis. My main -- the sources of information which I -- apart from my own eyes, which I thought were the best thing -- the best that I had in Sarajevo were, essentially, from international observers, from the International Committee of the Red Cross, and from UNHCR. We also would speak to various local sources, and as much as we could, when we heard something had happened, would try and get first-hand accounts. Now, I had first-hand accounts of what happened on the bus from people who were on the bus, from some of the adults who were accompanying the children across the front-line, and they told me that they had left Bosnian Government-controlled territory and were moving through on the road towards Ilidza when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the opportunity to check the information that you received?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, of course I checked it. I checked it by talking to different people to see if they came up with the same accounts. I mean, that's how you try to check information. I also saw -- I also went to the morgue where the two dead children's bodies were being kept. I wasn't able to go in there, but my cameraman, a BBC cameraman, went in there. They were only letting one person in. And he got pictures of the bodies, which we -- we also cross-checked with the -- through clothing with pictures of kids who were on the bus. I mean, the fact of what happened is in no dispute. As I said before, my problem in my piece was that I -- I made a mistake about where the shooting came from. But if you look at the piece, it's clear that the bus is leaving Bosnian Government-controlled territory. And the following -- the day of that piece, the day after -- the kids were killed in the evening. The morning after, I spent a lot of time talking to people who had -- partly people -- international people who'd received information, UNPROFOR, UNHCR. I think we probably got the first notice of the killing from UNPROFOR, itself. They had, you know, quite a good press information setup. And then they -- the people from the Children's Embassy, which was a local NGO who were organising all of this, I spoke to them as well and got their accounts of what happened, including accounts from people who -- some of the adults who were accompanying those children as they -- as they went off on this ill-conceived rescue mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to bring into question the actual incidents; namely, that somebody fired at the bus and that two children fell victim. In paragraph 37, you say: [In English] "Presumably, Serb. A sniper, presumably Serb, as the bus was coming from Bosnian Government side, opened the fire." [Interpretation] Why did you assume that it was a Serb sniper shooter; on what grounds?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Because they were coming -- because they were out of Bosnian Government-controlled territory and they were approaching Serb-controlled territory. I think they were through the no-man's land, as far as I was informed. And the thing is, you know, it was an urban area. You know, as you know much better than me, you know, it's a fairly -- there's a bit of green space around there, but it's not like it's a mountainous or a forested area where people could move themselves in easily and get -- and get into a position where they could fire. I mean, they had left the territory, as I was informed by several sources, that was controlled by the Bosnian Government, and by a process of elimination you can say that they were getting -- they were -- they were either in or very close to Bosnian Serb-controlled territory. So I think that's why I said "presumably." What did I say -- and the words I used, "appeared to come from Serb positions," because it was physically hard to see how they could come from the Bosnian Government-controlled positions. The shooting came in through the side of the bus, I think, and just to, you know, physically get a shot into a bus from the side, then I think you need to be -- you need to be in the area where it's at at the time. So I felt that the -- I will absolutely willingly say that I was not there and I didn't see the incident with my own eyes, but the weight of circumstantial evidence, I felt as a journalist, based on what I saw and the people I spoke to and accounts from various sources of the incident, suggested to me that, as I say in my witness statement, that the bullets appeared to come from Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did any of your interlocutors tell you that the investigation showed that it was the Serbs that had done the firing or was that your own assessment?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was my own assessment based on things they said to me. And their assessments were going in the same direction as well. I think at that point, and you're talking about hours after the incident, there certainly hadn't been any kind of formal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you find out whether any subsequent investigations proved that it was the Serbs who had done the shooting?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I never went back to follow up the shooting. Perhaps it's something we should have done. But at the time, as you'll remember, in July 1992, a lot was happening, and I was there not to make a documentary and look into depth -- in depth at particular incidents. I was there to cover daily news as it happened. And at the time, we were sending pieces to the BBC two, maybe three times a day. There was a huge appetite for what was happening in Sarajevo. So we did that piece, and then, essentially, by the weight of events, were forced to move on. I think that if it had gone very quiet, then we may well have gone into some deeper investigation but because there was, you know, a big news story almost every day, sadly it wasn't possible to go back. But I would stand by what I said, because I think that the -- the weight of the information that was coming to me pointed me in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we're discussing your primary task, allow me to remind you what you said in paragraph 6 of your amalgamated statement. You said that you were out in the field, that you reported from many other countries. [In English] "Because I tried wherever possible to illustrate how war affected the civilian population, rather than just reporting the doings of soldiers." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. One of the characteristics of warfare in the 20th century, and there are figures that you can find about this -- sorry, I don't have the precise ones with me. But if you look at warfare at the end of the 19th century, the beginning of the 20th century, the majority of people who died in wars then were military. If you look at wars now, by far the majority -- and 20 years ago in the Balkans, you'll find that by far the majority of people who die are civilians. So, therefore, they suffer most in wars, they're most caught up in it. So it's not simply -- it's not at all a prurient interest in human suffering. What it is is it's a reflection of the way that war is waged these days. Military forces tend to be much better protected, and civilians suffer, therefore, disproportionately. So I think that that's a very good reason for featuring them quite heavily in my reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're on the subject: What is your estimate? How many victims were there in the Bosnian war?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I never made account of that myself. I'm aware of the different estimates that were being used at the time. I think a common estimate around the mid-1990s was 200.000. I think that may have been revised downwards, but I'm no authority on the big picture, numbers of casualties. I know that there have been -- that various estimates are around. I think -- I know, myself, from experience elsewhere, Iraq, for example, it's very difficult to assess precisely how many people are killed over a period of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I hope that we do agree that those Serbs were not responsible for anything that happened in Iraq. However, if I were to tell you that the Muslim Institute, the Bosnian Institute, as it's called, established that there were 97.000 victims in this war on all three sides, and if I put it to you that the Muslims waged war against the Serbs and against the Croats and against Abdic, and that, as such, they had about 40.000 soldiers who were killed, because that is the number of sites they had ordered, so the number of Muslim civilians is almost three times less than the number of soldiers. About 30.000 Serbs were killed, about 10.000 Croats, so if you put all of this together, it was about 65.000 Muslims, out of which about 40.000 soldiers. So you see the figures don't seem to match there.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, I can't possibly answer that question because I'm not an authority on the figures and that's your interpretation of them. I haven't made any study of the figures. At no point in my evidence, either, did I think -- I talked about -- I didn't talk about large numbers of casualties or make any attempt to state what the numbers of dead were. So, as I say, I'm sorry, I can't -- I can't help you with that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to paragraph 6 of your statement. If, and that is quite noble, if you wanted to report on the suffering of civilians rather than just the doings of soldiers, then do you agree that you could have condemned war in a humanistic way, but you could not draw conclusions on the responsibility of either side; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'm an impartial BBC journalist. The idea of impartiality is absolutely central to the way that the BBC reports stories around the world. That's something which is not just in the Balkans, but in my current job in the Middle East, is something I have to work on the whole time. Being impartial is tough sometimes, but it's something that we have to do. It's not my business to do condemnation, but trying to be an impartial reporter doesn't mean that you say, Well, on the one hand, On the other hand, and, therefore, the truth is something in the middle or something like that. If you see things that are happening, and you see them yourself, and you have good evidence that they are happening, then you need to say that. And what I found in my reporting career, not just in the Balkans, though that was a good example of it, is that sometimes, as a reporter, you say things that one side or the other doesn't like, and, sadly, that's just the way things are. So my personal view about war is that it's abhorrent. I've seen a lot of war and a lot of death. But, you know, these reports, they're not about me; they're about people on the ground. They're not about my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the condemnation of war, I fully agree with you. You mentioned that people from UNPROFOR were often your sources of information. Are you familiar with the assessment of UNPROFOR commanders that the media did a very bad job and that they were highly partial in their reporting from Bosnia, and in this way, that they aggravated the situation altogether?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that assessment. There were different UNPROFOR commanders who had different ideas about the way that the media went on. You know, they're entitled to their views, if those, indeed, were their views. I don't think the media aggravated the situation. I don't think that we were players there. I think that we were passing on events, to the best of our ability, accurately and fairly, certainly as far as the BBC was concerned. I can't speak for other news organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that both UNPROFOR and others believed that there was a type of journalists who simply sat at hotels and bought, as it were, Muslim propaganda and propaganda from other sources, and then simply relayed that as information to their offices or desks? Were you among such journalists? Were you just sitting in Sarajevo, receiving footage filmed either by your own crews or other agency, and did you simply forward that to the BBC?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, that's not the way I do my business at all. Maybe there were journalists like that. I don't know, I didn't know them. And as I say, I can't speak for other journalists. But the ones who were close associates of mine, I think, worked very hard to be fair. And there was an ethos as well of going out there and seeing things for yourself. I wasn't just in Sarajevo; I went to many parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the period of the war. And I worked very hard, as I said earlier this morning, to try and report as much as I could from the Serb side, but, sadly, that wasn't possible because there were quite a bit of -- a few restrictions put on us. But, no, I was not somebody who sat in the hotel, received information, and then just pumped it out. That's not how I report. I have professional standards and professional pride, and I certainly wouldn't be doing things like that. And I think, quite frankly, if I did, I probably wouldn't last very long at the BBC, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had a single team or crew from reporting from the Serb side and the Muslim side or did you have separate teams?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It depended on the situation and on the -- and what was going on. There were times in the course of the war, at busy times especially, when the BBC would have a number of reporters and a number of cameramen in different places. But, generally speaking, because of the, you know, demands of the budget and the level of interest in the story, we probably had one team for most of the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were at different places. Some of my colleagues almost specialised in covering the doings of the British Army, for example, in UNPROFOR. I was keen always to get to grips with what was happening to Bosnians from all sides, so I wasn't very interested in going to Vitez to be with the British soldiers. I was more interested in going to Sarajevo, to other places as well, as much as I could to see what was happening on both sides -- on all sides, because I spent a lot of time with Muslims, Croats, and as much as I could with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any difficulties when it came to fulfilling the BBC demands, the demand being for you to report thoroughly, correctly and objectively about all of the three warring sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you ever have any problems with being objective, with favouring one party or the other?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I never favoured one party over the other, I never did. I actually grew to like people on all sides. And, you know, apart from the fact that the -- there was a terrible war going on, for me it was quite a privilege to get to know not just Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the former Yugoslavia. I tended to like the people there. I enjoyed spending time, particularly with all of them. But, you know, my time on the Serb side, I always enjoyed talking to Serbs and finding out how they ticked and spending time with them, you know, having a small toast with them or something like that, and I found -- I tended to find that once the initial suspicion had subsided, and I hoped to win their confidence a bit, that I was able to get on well with people. As for being, the earlier part of your question, did I have difficulties in filling BBC demands about being objective, no, I didn't. The problems that you face as a reporter in somewhere like Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war were all the problems of being in a war zone, the difficulties of trying to gather news in a place where it's very dangerous, where you have to worry about your own safety and those of your team, as well as all the other points of trying to get a good snap-shot that day of what's happening.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2937 is the next document I would like to present to the witness. This is another footage -- or, rather, a report involving children. Let's go back to that and let's clarify some things, since we're already talking about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No sound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No sound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have a transcript in order to be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the number, 65 ter number, for this clip?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 45372 something. And if I could have your indulgence for a couple of seconds, I should be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In 1D number, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2937.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's 45372A. Your Honours, it looks like Dr. Karadzic might have a technical problem because -- we could actually probably play that from here and broadcast it for him, if he wants to ask a question about it, but maybe the greater problem should be resolved by our colleagues in the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the nodding of Mr. Karadzic. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: The bus set off to cross the front-lines at about 6.30 yesterday evening. The children were tied to the seats so that they wouldn't be thrown around by the rough roads along the way. Their parents are missing or refugees. The plan was to reunite the families in Germany. "Our cameraman took this picture of 13-month-old Roki Sulejmanovic just before he left the bus as it approached no-man's land. A few minutes later, Roki and Vedrana Glavas, a three-year-old girl, were killed by the sniper. "The shooting happened a couple of hundred yards behind me. It's about the most dangerous stretch of road in Sarajevo, and they chose the most dangerous time of day to go down it. "Snipers hidden in these buildings which the Serbs control kill or wound people almost every day." "To me it borders on being criminally negligent to take children, or anyone else for that matter, into a known war zone at a time when the fighting starts every day." "Reporter: But the UN has been condemned here as well. It won't give --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, first we see the material from the bus, and your cameraman was on the bus. And then we see that the cameraman left the bus, and we see the bus leaving; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The cameraman was on the bus, and then there's a shot, as you saw, of the bus going through the check-point. And that was the last Bosnian Government check-point on that road going, I think, west out of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you say that -- can this footage be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As edited, as 1D2937 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- with sound. That can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D935, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D29197 [as interpreted] is the next document I would like the Court to produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that time -- or, rather, then the bus left the area under the control of the Muslim Army and arrived in the area of no-man's land; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was going through no-man's land, which, as you know, was not a very wide expanse, yeah, after it left, because you see it leaving.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... yesterday evening. The children were tied to the seats --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to replay that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, could you help us with the following: How far were the lines in Sarajevo from each other, and how long was the stretch of road going through the no-man's land? What was the normal distance between the enemy lines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, at some places, it was very close, and at other places, it was further apart. I actually went down -- in that period, we were able to take that road ourselves occasionally to go to Ilidza to buy fuel and to get supplies, so I went down it myself a few times. It wasn't far at all. You know, you left the last Bosnian check-point, and then, you know, within -- I can't give you a precise distance, but within a couple of minutes, a very short drive, you'd be seeing Bosnian Serb troops. So it was -- you know, you're talking -- the area that was controlled by the Bosnian Government was not large, really, in the great scheme of things, and that particular stretch of road, the terrain there is pretty flat. Yeah, and as I say, I found that travelling to Ilidza from the centre part of Sarajevo was -- it was probably -- it would feel like a couple of minutes' drive maximum, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that. Your cameraman, according to what he was told, depicted the "Oslobodjenje" building as a source of fire. You corrected yourself and you said that that should not have been a source of fire, because the building was under the control of the Bosnian Muslim army; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was under the control of the -- yeah, of that Muslim army, and I corrected that. I mean, I was misinformed at the time. I hadn't been in the city very long, and while over the period of years I got to know the geography I think quite well, very well. I always drove myself around. I didn't have a driver or anything like that. By that period in my first week or so, I didn't know it very well. So, frankly, you know, that was a complete -- it was a howler to suggest that there were Serb gunmen at that time in the "Oslobodjenje" building, because it was controlled by the government and they were producing their newspaper there on a daily basis. So, no, I've said -- I've held my hands up, I mean, that was a mistake that I made. But since you mention that, what I would say is that the distance from the place where the shooting happened to the "Oslobodjenje" building is quite considerable. From the building to the check-point, I think, is 300 or 400 metres, and then the bus would have been -- you know, would have driven for a while when the shooting happened. Had it happened quickly, the cameraman would have stayed and got the immediate aftermath, but he went. He couldn't have heard -- he would have stayed if he heard gun-fire. I know that. So you're talking about a long distance from the "Oslobodjenje" building, so just physically there's no way the shot could have come from there, which is why I made that correction at the beginning of proceedings here today, because I thought it was important to get that straight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2917 is the document that I would like to call up in e-court. This is a part of your book, "War Stories," and that part relates to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can we please look at page 163, but not in e-court, but in the book, 163 in the book. Could the technical booth please pay attention to the page number at the bottom of the page. It must be page 15 or thereabouts in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read -- or, rather, can you read the passage starting with: "I was convinced ..." The middle part of the second passage.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: From: "I was convinced ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the third sentence there.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I mean, I can read it from there, but I think it's important to read it at least from the beginning of the paragraph or you lose the context of that sentence. So if you don't mind, I'll read it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I was disgusted by what had happened and full of anger against the people who had done it." This is a reference, Your Honour, to the attack on the funeral. "The deaths of the children were a crime in themselves, but then to shell the funeral was another --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll start again: "I was disgusted by what had happened and full of anger against the people who had done it. The deaths of the children were a crime in themselves, but then to shell their funeral was another outrage. I was about to vent my anger in a piece to camera that laid into the Serbs for committing war crimes. I was convinced that the Serbs were responsible. A conspiracy theory was put around by some UN people that the Bosnian Government was in the habit of shelling their own people to get world sympathy and to make the Serbs look bad. I never saw any proof that it was true. And the graveyard was not just being shelled because the cameras were there; the gravediggers said it was shelled plenty of times when cameras were not there too. Then something in my mind, I suppose the training I had from the BBC, told me to hold on, to calm down, to think hard about what I was going to say, and to play it straight. I still think that was the right way to do it. The piece was more powerful because -- the piece was more powerful because the tone of it was more measured. I laid out the facts and the pictures about what had happened, and --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, thank you. We already said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is this: We agree that that was awful, I am disgusted, but what was the basis for you to believe that that was done by the Serbs, and why did you reject the UN theory that the Muslims were shelling their own people? What made you reject that theory, and what made you believe that it had been the Serbs? How come that you finally recorded that in your book?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Starting, first of all, with the -- with the funeral, itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, we'll come to the funeral, we'll come to the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is about the funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, let's talk about the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you establish that it was the Serbs who shot at the bus? How did you come to reject the theory that that could have been done by Muslim soldiers or, rather, the government, although the theory was supported by the UN?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
