utterances.text: At that point, I hadn't heard the theory that the Bosnian Government side were doing it to their own people. I first heard the theory from a military aide to General Lewis MacKenzie, who was the UNPROFOR Sarajevo Sector commander at the time, towards the end of that first visit I paid to Sarajevo, which was August of 1992. So he took me to one side and said, Look, by the way, I want you to know we're convinced that the Serbs -- sorry, that the Bosnian Government are shelling themselves. So I said, Well, what evidence have you got? And he said, We don't really have any evidence, but that's what we think. Now, your earlier part of the question, where you asked me, How did you establish it was the Serbs who shot at the bus, you'll say -- you'll see we went through my statement earlier on, and in that I think I was effectively saying that the balance of probabilities were that the Serbs shot at the bus. And to repeat what I said, that was based on where the bus was, it was based as well -- well, it was based principally on where the bus was, that it had left Bosnian Serb-controlled territory. And as you said your -- and as I said in answer to your question just now, the geographical distance between the final Bosnian Government check-point and the first Bosnian Serb check-point was not very great at all. Again, it's -- there's a lot of circumstantial evidence there. I didn't see it with my own eyes, I didn't have ballistics tests about the weapons that were fired and so on, but it just seemed -- judging by where it had got to, the fact that the bus had left, the camera crew had left, that it was some way through, and that was an area controlled by Bosnian Serbs. So had they wanted to shoot at it themselves, it would have made more sense if, indeed, they had shot, say, from the "Oslobodjenje" building, but that didn't happen. So, as I say, I felt that the -- you know, it wasn't 100 per cent, but the balance of -- well, not 100 per cent, because I hadn't seen it, but the balance of probability, as I said in my -- in the language -- I chose my language carefully in the witness statement, was that the Serbs had been responsible for that particular attack. And I would absolutely repeat again what I said in that book, that I thought it was a terrible crime that children were being killed in that way, and also I thought it was equally criminal that their funerals were shelled. I thought it was grotesquely violent and cruel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I totally agree with you, but let's prove who actually did it. Your Excellency, is it enough to have what is on the transcript or should this page be tendered into evidence? I'm asking the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no opposition. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D936, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see in e-court 65 ter 09390-C. I believe that the document must have a P number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll start with the first page first, and then -- or, rather, we'll start with the second page after the title page, and then we'll move to section 9. Can this be turned clockwise by 90 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this map, Mr. Bowen? Is this Sarajevo, and are the lines depicted? Do you agree that the event happened in the map section number 9, that the "Oslobodjenje" building is also there, and that the place where the event happened is also there? Do you see the main road leading from Sarajevo to Ilidza? There are some numbers there as well.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The screen's gone. Okay. At the moment, it's -- can you make it big again? I'm just seeing the whole map, not -- don't touch it? Okay, right. I didn't realise it was a touch screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the main road now? Do you see the main road leading from Sarajevo to --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Is the road the red line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid that the red and the blue lines are the front-lines, if you will agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I don't mean the broken red or blue lines. I'm talking about -- I can see -- I'm assuming the black lines on the map are railway lines, are they, or are they roads? They're roads, then, are they, the black lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, both the rail lines and the roads are black. You can see three dots and numbers there. However, do you recognise the "Oslobodjenje" building closest to the front-line? Could Mr. Bowen be provided with a pen. Maybe that would assist him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we see sheet 9 of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I'm looking at -- the buildings aren't marked. Is it -- can I touch it? Oh, okay. Is it -- could you possibly -- sir, could you ring the "Oslobodjenje" building? Is it this building here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid it is more to the south. Do you see the lines closest to the road?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Excuse me. Your answer was overlapped with the translation, so it's not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- properly translated. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lines closest to -- I'm not clear, sir, about which lines you're referring to. If, perhaps, you could mark on the map yourselves which ones you're referring to, it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to pay attention to the lower third of the map. You can see the two jutted lines close to the road. Do you see the lower third or, rather, the right-hand side corner, the lower portion, the lower third, the right-hand side portion? Do you see the star-like buildings in the right-hand side corner? Those were students' dormitories. Do you remember that? Did you know where Nedzarici was? That was a Serbian neighbourhood, Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew of Nedzarici. But the point is that I'm not -- when you're referring to these various places on the map, I'm not following, really, what you're saying. I'm sorry. I never had this particular map when I was there, and my sense of geography was based very much on driving up and down the roads. I never had a map of this -- sadly, of this accuracy and quality, so, you know, I had a driver's eye view of the place. So you're going to have to -- if you want me to be specific about things, I'm going to have to see it marked on the map, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's try this: Do you see two star-like buildings by the line on the right-hand side which delineates the whole section 9? Those were student dormitories. Do you remember those buildings?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The -- if I saw them, I might remember them, if I saw a picture of them. But star-like buildings, do you mean the -- there's some crosses which are next to the thick blue line delineating section 9. Just on the right of it, is that the ones that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Going towards Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can write letters. Y, actually. Can you circle those two buildings? They are the dorms that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Can I circle them? I'm sorry if I'm being a bit thick here, but I'm not following you. I'm normally not bad with maps, but I can't -- I'm struggling a bit here. I'm very anxious that I'm accurate in what I say to you, so perhaps if someone could point these out to me on the map by a circle or something, it would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm now wondering whether it would be helpful to continue this exercise, given the unfamiliarity of the witness with the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, can you see where the Muslims' end stops and the Serb zone continues? That happens on the road, black road with tram stops marked along the road. Can you perhaps mark that? And that's the road that starts cutting through the middle of the section and then abruptly continues southward.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Are you referring to this road here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the very far south, on the exact opposite side. What you are pointing at is Zadar, in the north, and what I am referring to is the area close to Nedzarici, on the south.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, so down here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really wondering about the utility of this now, especially when we get to the discussion of where the confrontation lines might have laid because this map is and these lines are based on confrontation lines as depicted in maps from 1995 and this whole line of questioning relates to an incident in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, the confrontation lines didn't change. The only part that changed was Otes. The rest of the lines remained the same throughout the war, and Mr. Bowen confirmed that in his statement. He confirmed that the lines remained almost unchanged until the very end of the war. But now I'm looking at the section of the road where the incident with the bus took place, and that's the road that we are supposed to identify and see how was it possible to conclude that the incident had been caused by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Bowen has said in his testimony, in his cross-examination, that he wasn't there and he didn't see it, so I'm really wondering what the utility of this is altogether. And he said that, for the record, at page 82, line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think you exhausted the issue when you asked some questions about that incident already. I would recommend you to move on to your next topic. I don't see any utility, as indicated by Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness, with a lot of authority, reported on BBC and repeated in his book that that was done by the Serbs in no-man's land, and here no-man's land is only 50 metres away from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, how come you concluded that it must have been the Serbs who had shot from no-man's land? Was it from no-man's land that they fired the shots from or from the Serb-held territory? Where should this have been done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Bowen has answered the question already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can add one clarification, if you like, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, if you're saying yourself that no-man's land is very narrow there, then it could -- then I could say that, in a sense, I was trying to be as fair as I could by saying it looked like no-man's land. But we have a picture of the bus going through the final Bosnian check-point and heading off down the road, and at that point the bus was as yet unmolested and not shot at by anybody. Now, you said yourself that it was a small distance between the two positions. That suggests to me that if it wasn't no-man's land, it would have been in Serb territory that the attack took place, and that's -- because it would be some minutes, I would imagine, after they left. Otherwise, the camera crew would have heard shooting and probably would have stayed, because I know the guys who shot that and they would, you know, they wouldn't have just run away from it. So if no-man's land was narrow, the bus would have already passed through it and be in Serb territory, and then the attack would have happened, because what is absolutely clear from the pictures is that the attack did not happen in Bosnian Government-controlled territory. So I would say that from what you're saying, it was -- my assumption was no-man's land or going towards the Serb side, and now from what you're saying or suggesting to me that it might actually be in Serb territory, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was it that you went? Where was this morgue where the killed children were?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It wasn't the main morgue that was at the Kosevo Hospital, where many of the bodies were taken. It was more of an improvised morgue in -- I suppose it was something that was once a store room. So if you -- my recollection is that -- and, you know, it's 19 years ago, but my recollection is that it was either on or just off that main road that went in -- if you turned the other way and went past the "Oslobodjenje" building and continued along that road, either on the left -- if you went left and the roads there, it was one of those, I think, but it was a small local place where the bodies were being held. At that point, they hadn't been taken -- I don't know if they were ever taken to the morgue at Kosevo Hospital, where quite a few of the bodies were taken of civilians and also of fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: We had -- I'm trying to remember. We had a local fixer, a local resident, and who was a surgeon, as a matter of fact, at the hospital, and she found out -- I think she made some phone calls. She got some information about where the bodies had been taken. And so, therefore, we wanted to go and find out. And, you know, and she also asked at check-points. There were quite a lot of check-points. She asked -- we asked around, essentially, to try to get the information. And then we went there, and there were the bodies of the children.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this once again -- actually, there is nothing to be admitted here. 1D2917, but page 161, could we have that now, please. 1D2917 is the previous document, but it's just one page down in e-court, page 161. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Our cameraman filmed the children as the bus drove towards the last Bosnian check-point at the edge of town, where he got off. The bus went on into no-man's land, where a sniper, presumably a Serb, as the bus was coming from the government side, opened fire." [Interpretation] Is this the basis for your conclusion, namely, because the bus is coming from the Bosnian side, that is why the Serbs were the ones that fired, or are you relying on something else?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I mean, I've gone already, I'd say, into more detail about why I made that supposition. In the book, itself, it was not necessary or advisable to go into that kind of detail that you would in a court of law. I mean, I think I've explained already why I came to that conclusion. And what's there in parenthesis in that sentence is a -- it's a shorthand version. I think I've already gone through what I think happened, and I've -- and I've -- throughout my reporting and also in the book, I've laid open a -- you know, a possibility not about necessarily what happened but more about the fact that I have incomplete knowledge of the event, because that's why I use the word "presumably." I never tried to hide the fact that I wasn't there. And so, no, that's what I can say about that point, that's how I respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see the next paragraph: [In English] "The two children were taken to a mortuary not far from the place where the bus trip started." [Interpretation] Was that mortuary on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was on the Muslim side. It was on the Muslim side -- Muslim-led side, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Knowing the check-points and the lines, and the control of movements, as such, could you explain how the dead bodies of children who had been killed on the Serb side could eventually be brought to a mortuary on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, that was one reason why my assumption was it was no-man's land initially, because the bus turned 'round. From memory, I think there were pictures, which we didn't use, of the bus after it had been shot up, because the bus -- they turned 'round and they came back in, because the adults and the driver on the bus were people who'd come from the Bosnian Government-controlled part of the city, so I guess their first instincts when this thing happened was to turnaround and go back the way they came. I think it was probably a flight reflex, because as well as having two dead children on the bus, they had -- well, you saw from the pictures yourself, they were probably getting on with 20 small children, many of whom were tied to the seats because otherwise they might have fallen off. They weren't even big enough to sit independently. So I think that, yes, what happened was they turned around and they came back in, and that's why the bodies and the funerals were there on the Bosnian Government side. And, you know, as I say, there's a picture in the report of the bus going through the final Bosnian Government check-point, so I think we can establish from that that it left their zone of control and then it went back into it after the shooting incident, and whatever point on the road it had got to when the shots happened, and my information was it was pretty soon after they'd gone through the check-point, they were able maybe -- I mean, I didn't speak to the driver and ask him, Did you immediately do a three-point turn or a U-turn and go back? But I think it was apparent, because the bus was back in town, that that's what had happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can page 161 be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be added to the previous exhibit, D936. In the meantime, Mr. Bowen, there must have been a check-point on the Serb side after no-man's land on that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was, and I don't know whether it had passed that check-point when the attack happened or whether it was approaching the check-point. But as you can see from the map, the distances between the confrontation lines were not great, Your Honour, so it can't have got very far when the -- when that shooting incident took place. And I don't know if they crossed -- you know, sometimes on check-points there wouldn't even be people there all the time. There might be a little bit in the background. So, as I say, I wasn't there when the incident happened, so this is, you know, supposition on my part. I don't really want to speculate too much about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The funeral took place at the Lav Cemetery; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: At the -- well, the Lav -- we always referred to it as the Lion's Cemetery, but, yes, the main cemetery which had the sculpture of a lion in it, which was just below Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at this again now, 65 ter 09390-C, and then let's look at section 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do I remember this right, that you said that it was either the funeral itself or a visit to the cemetery, it seems, that it was actually a visit to the cemetery, and the flowers were brought, and shells were falling, and somebody was actually hit in the head by a rifle bullet; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, that's -- no. If you're referring to the funerals of the two dead children who were involved in the bus incident, it was their funeral, and what I reported was -- we were given a time that the funeral was going to take place, and we arrived a little bit early for that and found that the funeral had happened already, and that's because, as I intimated in the report, that the grave-diggers and the people at the cemetery, I think principally the grave-diggers, had decided just to go ahead and bury the bodies before the mourners arrived because of the shelling. At that point when the shelling first started, there were no mourners there were. There were just the grave-diggers who, you know how it works, they prepare the hole and then the funeral happens, and -- but by the time we got there, and, as I say, it was before the scheduled time for the funeral, that that had already taken place. So after we got there, the kids arrived from the children's home, where these young children had been living, with flowers that they wanted to put down, so they were there because of a funeral. It wasn't just any old visit, and they were specifically there because of the funeral of those children. And nobody was shot in the head. What the video depicts is the grandmother of the dead girl who -- she sustained very nasty shrapnel injury in her upper arm. I think it was her left arm. You can see from the video, anyway. Yeah, I'm pretty sure it was left. And she had a very large hole in it which, when my colleague, Kurt Schork, who was in charge of the -- he took charge of the first aid there, and you see me coming into the picture, giving them a second field dressing. He had one field dressing. He put it into the hole in her arm, and the hole was so big, the dressing disappeared into the hole. So I gave them my field dressing, and that's on the video, and they put that field dressing on top of that second -- of that first field dressing in a bid to stop what was very severe bleeding coming. And then we took her to the hospital, which is only a minute's or so drive away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we try page 9 of this document. And what is your question, Mr. Karadzic, about this map, page 9 of this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we need this number 7 so that Mr. Bowen could -- oh, all right. Can we enlarge this central part, where it says "Cemetery," so that we could ask Mr. Bowen -- further up, further up to the north. Yes, that's right, fine. Excellent, great.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see what it says here, one, two, three, "Cemetery." There's the Catholic cemetery, the Orthodox cemetery, and further up, right by the hospital, the Kosevo Hospital, is the Lion's Cemetery, "Lav," L-a-v?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see those three cemeteries there. Yeah, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put a circle around the Lion's Cemetery?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Which is the Lion's Cemetery? Is that the middle one or the one at the top? This one, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The one on the top, by the hospital, itself.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Next to the sports fields. It spread over into the sports field as the war continued, because they ran out of room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put the date there? Could you say L for the Lion's Cemetery, and the date and your initials, please?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The L for "Lion," yeah. Today's date? Today's date is, what, the 12th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bottom right. Yes, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 13th January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "13/1," sorry, "1/11" [marks]. And my initials, J.B. -- sorry, it's not easy to write with these pens.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be admitted now, however -- THE COURT: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I took my seat again because Dr. Karadzic continued, but if it's to be admitted, it's a document at the direction and at the instruction of Dr. Karadzic by the witness. Dr. Karadzic was the one who specifically indicated the location of the cemetery to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the witness did confirm the location, didn't he? Mr. Bowen, you confirm the location of the Lav Cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I say, you know, as I said before I didn't have maps when I was in Sarajevo. So I used to -- I mean, I could drive you there, if you wanted. But as far as I can see from this map, based on the fact that there were athletic fields next to it and then you could see the stadium over close by, I do remember, as you came along, there was another cemetery on the left, and then there was -- yes, so I think that's the Lion's Cemetery, certainly, and the buildings up to the -- I spilled the water. And the buildings up to the right are the hospital, I suppose. Can I have some tissues? I just knocked my glass of water over everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's behind your monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry about this. It's all gone a bit fuzzy now in my ear piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit this in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D937, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If necessary, we can play that footage again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that there was a gunman firing there; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I used the word "gunman," because I don't think I used the word. I mean, I'd have to look at it again. No, my deduction about Serbs being responsible for it at the time was based on the fact that there had been regular shelling of the cemetery, which we have from numerous sources and had colleagues at the scene as well, and I had conversations with people -- with military people about where it could be coming from, and it was clear that it was in -- it was in the range of the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I misunderstood that. It was my understanding that you had said "gunman" and that somebody had sustained a rifle wound. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A correction. The term used by that report was "gunners."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, it was "gunners," sorry, "gunners," not "gunmen." I beg your pardon, "gunners" being a generic term for artillerymen. I wasn't -- yeah. Of course, that was the ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have P815, or, actually, that map, but could we see all of this map. Can we see the totality of this map, not just this section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you agree that one confrontation line follows another confrontation line here?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The confrontation lines followed each other right 'round the city, yes. You can see from the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order for the Serbs to fire, they would have to be firing from their own territory, that is to say, outside the red confrontation line; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then comes the blue line, and the Muslim trenches, and then Muslim-held territory that is fully under their control; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, inside the blue line was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can we conclude, without ballistic expertise and a proper investigation, that it was a particular side that had fired, that it wasn't either one of the two sides?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I had already had discussions with people about the fact that the graveyard was getting shelled, and -- people inside UNPROFOR, and the -- I think they pointed out positions to me which were north of where the cemetery was, and they thought -- their assumption was that shells were coming in from there. There's also the question of motive, and I think it's important that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just could you wait?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we mark the position you were in at the time, roughly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Somewhere in -- you know, up there. I wouldn't go into specifics about it, because I don't have that accurate information, but it's quite close by and people -- those are the kinds of discussions I had. And also the point I was going to go on to make, if I may, Your Honour, was that it's a question of motive. The supposition that the Bosnian Government side was shelling its own people is based on the fact that they wanted to make an incident that would play internationally, that would show the Serbs in a bad light. Now, on that particular day, the shelling was happening when there were no cameras there, and on other days -- and you can see the damage in the cemetery, and we didn't have cameras there every day. I can tell you that that graveyard was often shelled. I don't see why -- if, let's say for one second -- and I don't accept the point, but say for one second the Bosnian Government wanted to make an international incident, why would they shell it when the television cameras weren't there? Plus there's another point in retrospect, but I think it's relevant, that it's been nearly 20 years. They weren't well organised, especially in 1992. No information has ever emerged to confirm that the Bosnian Government shelled its own side. There hasn't been any. During the war, the UNPROFOR people engaged in a great deal of crater analysis, and to my -- and maybe something is top secret, but to my knowledge, there was nothing definitive that ever came out of that. And, you know, most importantly, it's been nearly 20 years. It's very hard to cover things up for that length of time. And there has not, as far as I'm aware, been one definitive bit of information, the smoking gun, if you like, saying that the Bosnian people shelled their own side. The Americans were unable in Iraq to keep Abu Ghraib and what they did there a secret for longer than about 12 months, maybe less than that. To my mind, something would have come out by now if this was the case. So I think that our suppositions, based on the information that we had at the time, which I will agree were incomplete and circumstantial, and there was the fog of war to think about as well, but in all the years of peace since then, since the Dayton Agreement, no specific evidence that I'm aware of has come out suggesting -- confirming these repeated allegations that the Bosnian Government shelled its own side to try to manipulate the media. I don't think it stands up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you then marked the Lion's Cemetery on this map? You remember that it's by the Kosevo Hospital and opposite the stadium, so let us see what the scale is.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think around there, more or less. That's about -- from the red line, at that point -- the closest point to the red line is just over a kilometre, according to the scale at the bottom of the map. And in the other direction, it's, what, just over two, probably. And don't forget that the Serb side there is high ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put the date in. Initial on the bottom right part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did we say it was the 13th? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 13 January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone inform you that a certain azimuth existed, or, rather, that there was a certain angle, in view of how this shell fell? Did anybody give you any ballistic information whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, not that technically. I knew that the shell fell, because I was there when it exploded and I saw what it did to the flesh. I spent -- not on that northern side, but on the southern side, I spent quite a bit of time and did some reporting which was broadcast with the Bosnian Serb forces who were there, and they -- I spoke to them about their activities in shelling the city. They said that they did it. I saw the empty shell casings. They allowed us to take a shot that was down the barrel of the gun -- of one of their heavy machine-guns, and it was close enough to the city to be able to hit it with a 50-calibre machine-gun. They also had anti-aircraft -- I'm not sure of the calibre, but anti-aircraft cannon which they depressed from the high altitude on the hills and used it as a ground attack weapon. And I spoke to the soldiers. I wasn't referring to this specific incident, I must stress. But the principle that the Serb fighters were shelling the city, as I say, I spoke to Serb fighters, themselves, I saw the empty shell cases, I was able to film them, it was broadcast. To my mind, you know, one of the big military advantages that the Serb side had around -- particularly to the north and to the south was that they held the high ground, and that made it quite possible -- you know, I could practically -- from the Serb positions to the south, I could practically see inside the hotel where I was staying at the Holiday Inn, and while I in it the building was hit a few times and it was quite badly damaged. So, no, I didn't have precise ballistic information, but I was aware of the general pattern of behaviour, in terms of the way that the siege was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be it for today, and the last map marked by the witness will be admitted as Exhibit D938. Before we adjourn, Mr. Tieger, were you able to contact the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to respond to the Court's inquiry, Your Honour. Of course, I could do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the absence of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's most appropriate. I'm not overly concerned about it, but it's probably the most useful thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bowen. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. You may be excused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in the meantime, we'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
